title: Could a 'thinking cap' make me a genius?
summary: Josh and Chuck examine whether a 'thinking cap' (transcranial magnetic stimulation, TMS) could make people geniuses. They open with a horrific New York twin-separation nature-versus-nurture study sealed until 2026 (Peter Neubauer's study), then discuss autistic savants (Kim Peek, the inspiration for Rain Man; Blind Tom), left-hemisphere damage and savant abilities, and Allan Snyder's theory of mindsets and latent inhibition. Snyder uses TMS on normal people, reportedly improving drawing, prime number recognition and proofreading temporarily, though the effects last about an hour and are not firmly established. TMS has also been FDA-approved for depression. The episode closes with an announcement of new How Stuff Works blogs and a listener mail about dust behavior in the moon landing episode, with a MythBusters laser-reflector reference.

segments.title: Opening banter and twin separation study
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with casual banter about Chuck's hat, then Josh describes a sealed New York study that separated adopted twins and triplets for nature versus nurture research, led by child psychologist Peter Neubauer, with results sealed at Yale until 2026.

segments.title: Savants and autistic savants
segments.summary: The hosts introduce savants, people with deficits who excel in particular areas, citing music savants, Blind Tom, and Kim Peek, the inspiration for Rain Man. They note savants are not always autistic and vice versa, and discuss Kim Peek's reading and memory abilities and his care.

segments.title: Left hemisphere damage and Snyder's mindset theory
segments.summary: Savants often have left-hemisphere damage, making them a natural experiment on brain lateralization, with the left side handling detail and the right the big picture. Allan Snyder at the Center for the Mind in Sydney proposes that mindsets are formed from experience, and that latent inhibition filters out familiar stimuli, a process impaired in schizophrenia.

segments.title: TMS experiments on normal people
segments.summary: TMS, originally used to examine brain function during surgery, was noticed by Snyder to cause temporary cognitive effects. Snyder applies it to normal subjects, reportedly improving drawing, prime number recognition and proofreading for about an hour. The hosts call it a 'thinking cap' and note skepticism about the claims.

segments.title: TMS for depression and stroke research
segments.summary: The hosts note that TMS was FDA-approved for depression, with a Philadelphia study of 300 patients where those treated were twice as likely to achieve remission. Stroke victims are being recruited for studies, and high-frequency TMS on the frontal lobe is said to restructure neurons. They speculate on use for smarter people.

segments.title: Takeaway on genius
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh conclude that TMS will not make a person a genius, and that savant-like skills are less special than they seem.

segments.title: How Stuff Works blog announcement
segments.summary: Chuck announces new How Stuff Works blogs, including a Stuff You Should Know blog for shorter topics and show announcements, and asks listeners to get involved.

segments.title: Listener mail on moon landing dust
segments.summary: Listener Jason corrects the hosts on dust behavior in the moon landing episode: dust on the Moon hangs longer due to low gravity, and air resistance has little effect on dust particles on Earth, so a vacuum sound stage is unnecessary. The hosts also reference MythBusters' laser reflector test confirming the landing.
